# How the Causal Impact dashboard works — end-to-end

A top-to-bottom read for someone who wants to understand **the statistics**: what each method computes, and what every chart in the dashboard shows and how its number is made. Part 1 is a short sketch of how the data flows, Part 2 is the methodology (the two causal methods), and Part 3 walks the dashboard chart by chart. For *current status* and *how to operate/deploy* it, see [README.md](README.md); for *why we diverge from the gold standard* (the methodology canon), see [DRIFT.md](DRIFT.md).

## What it answers

MNTN often ships a feature as a **BETA rollout** (flipping it on for a wave of advertisers, with no in-experiment holdout) rather than as a controlled A/B test. This dashboard standardizes a more robust way to measure **"what did a rollout actually cause?"**, and offers two different statistical approaches to that measurement. 

Adding a new feature to the dashboard requires providing 
1. What advertisers were affected 
2. What day they flipped 
3. What types of campaigns will be affected (eg. "Prospecting Campaigns" or "Campaigns that use a CRM block").

The unit of analysis is the **advertiser**. Because a feature usually touches only *some* of an advertiser's campaigns, a per-feature **scope recipe** resolves the in-scope `campaign_group_id`s once (at seed time). Performance is measured by summing performance across all relevant campaign groups for that advertiser, and observing the advertiser x day level metrics. This method is both statistically preferred and conveniently helps account for short flight campaign advertisers where instead of 10 disparate choppy campaign flights with broken performance ramps, we see a cohesive line of the collective performance across all of the relevant campaigns.

---

## Part 1 — how the data flows (the short version)

```
config  ─▶  SQL panels  ─▶  notebook (BSTS + DiD)  ─▶  dashboard (3 views)
```

Four stages, but **all the statistics happen in one of them** (the notebook, Part 2). The rest just gets clean daily counts in and renders the results out.

### Config 
Provides all the details and parameters about the feature
 - Names the experiment
 - Which advertisers were treated and when they flipped
 - Which campaigns the feature touched (the *scope*)
 - An optional untreated *control* advertisers/ campaigns
 - A row of tunable **knobs** (window lengths, maturity, eligibility thresholds, all detailed in Part 2). 
 - One parameter, the `Experiment Key`, selects it all
 - Onboarding a new feature to the dashboard just requires a config seed, not a full code change.

### SQL Panels
 - Uses the parameters provided from the config tables to query all relevant performance data
 - Attribution is made **UI-faithful** so the numbers match what the customer sees in the MNTN UI.

### The Notebook
 This is where the causal work happens:
  - It runs the eligibility gate on advertisers with too little data
  - Runs both methods (BSTS + DiD) on every metric performance metric
  - Writes out per-advertiser and per-cohort effect estimates with intervals.

### The Dashboard
Renders those estimates as three color-coded views
 - BSTS
 - Difference-in-Differences
 - 3-Point


> **How it's wired (for maintainers).** The moving parts are a set of config tables in `dw-main-silver.experiments.*`, seven parameterized SQL panels, a ~23-cell Python notebook (statsmodels + numpy/pandas; no `causalimpact` library), and one self-contained HTML file that reads the notebook's outputs as Mode "datasets." The exact table / column / dataset names, row counts, scan cost, and the deploy runbook live in [README.md](README.md) (status table + "Deploy to Mode") and [config/SCHEMA-DIAGRAM.md](config/SCHEMA-DIAGRAM.md). Those specifics are deliberately out of this doc, which is about the statistics.

## Part 2 — The Notebook workflow

Two methods run every refresh. 

1. **BSTS** builds a synthetic counterfactual by *forecast* (no control group needed)
2. **DiD** compares treated growth against a control group's growth. 

### BSTS — Bayesian Structural Time Series

BSTS answers *"what would this metric have done if the feature had never flipped?"* by **forecasting** that no-flip world from the treated group's own history, then comparing what actually happened against the forecast. A model is trained on data **before-the-flip**. We can optionally provide **control-group covariate data** that supports the model training by tracking the wider market than just the treatment.

#### **One cohort, step by step (metric = IVR):**

1. **Build the daily rate.** Each day, add up every advertiser in the cohort to form a daily rate: IVR = total visits ÷ total impressions. To be clear, this means it sums up one IVR per day to make a daily series.
2. **Train on the before-period.** Fit the model to the pre-flip part of that series. It learns to describe the rate as a sum of three pieces: a slow-moving **baseline level**, a repeating **weekly (day-of-week) pattern**, and (if control covariate data was supplied) a **market piece** that captures how this group's rate tracks the untreated market. Fitting simply sizes each piece so the sum reproduces the pre-flip days as closely as possible.
3. **Forecast the counterfactual.** Project that fitted description across the post-flip days, using each day's real weekday and real market values but no treatment. The result is the **counterfactual**: the model's best guess of the no-flip rate for each post-flip day (the dashed line in the Actual vs Counterfactual chart).
4. **Read the effect.** Average the actual rate and the counterfactual rate across the post-flip days; the effect is their ratio minus one, $(\text{avg actual} \div \text{avg counterfactual}) - 1$. A positive number means the flip pushed the metric above where the forecast said it would sit.
5. **Get the uncertainty.** The real pre-flip rate never sat exactly on the model's description; it wobbled, and the model measures how much. To create the interval of alternative counterfactuals, it **re-simulates the counterfactual ~2,000 times**, each a slightly different but plausible no-flip path. After each counterfactual simulation, we calculate the difference relative to the actual performance (the same way described in `4.`) to generate the full upper and lower bounds. By dropping the most extreme 2.5% at each end, we get the **95% confidence interval** (say **+3% to +11%**). The only test is whether that span contains the number **0**: if the whole span sits on one side of zero (as +3% to +11% does), nearly every simulation agreed on the direction, so the effect is **significant**; if the span straddles zero (say **−2% to +11%**), a true effect of "nothing" is still plausible, so it is **not** significant. *(The counterfactual line and the day-by-day band are drawn out in Part 3, CI-2.)*

#### **Multiple cohorts (waves that flipped on different dates):**

First, each cohort gets its **own** fit on its **own** flip date: sum its advertisers into one daily series, fit BSTS on that cohort's pre-flip days, forecast the post-flip counterfactual, and simulate ~2,000 no-flip paths (steps 1 to 5, once per cohort). So each cohort arrives carrying, for every post-flip day: an **actual rate**, a **counterfactual rate**, that day's **volume** (the denominator, e.g. impressions), and ~2,000 simulated counterfactual rates.

To combine them, line the cohorts up on a shared **flip clock** (day-since-flip, so every cohort's flip is day 1) and pool in two stages:

1. **Within a day, pool across cohorts by volume.** At day-since-flip *k*, add up every live cohort's actual count (rate × volume) and divide by their total volume for one pooled actual rate; same for the counterfactual. Bigger cohorts pull the pooled rate toward themselves, and a younger cohort that hasn't reached day *k* yet just isn't in that day's pool.
2. **Across days, average with equal weight.** Take the plain mean of those pooled daily rates over the event-days, once for actual and once for counterfactual. The effect is **(avg pooled actual ÷ avg pooled counterfactual) − 1**. Equal-weighting the days (rather than volume-weighting them) matches the single-cohort recipe in step 4, so a one-cohort "All Treated" reproduces that cohort's own bar exactly.

Worked, two cohorts, metric = IVR (visits ÷ impressions; `impr` is the volume weight):

```
Day 1:  Cohort A  actual 0.10, cf 0.08, impr 3000
        Cohort B  actual 0.20, cf 0.15, impr 1000
        pooled actual = (0.10×3000 + 0.20×1000) ÷ 4000 = 0.125
        pooled cf     = (0.08×3000 + 0.15×1000) ÷ 4000 = 0.0975

Day 2:  same volumes → pooled actual 0.125, pooled cf 0.0975

Day 3:  Cohort B not live yet, so Cohort A only
        pooled actual = 0.11, pooled cf = 0.08

Across days (equal weight):  actual = mean(0.125, 0.125, 0.11) = 0.120
                             cf     = mean(0.0975, 0.0975, 0.08) = 0.0917
effect = 0.120 ÷ 0.0917 − 1 = +30.9%
```

**The interval.** Each cohort brought ~2,000 simulated counterfactual paths, so pool them the exact same way: for each draw, blend the cohorts' counterfactual rates on the flip clock (volume within day, equal weight across days) into one pooled counterfactual average, giving ~2,000 of them. The observed actual never moves, so dividing it by each draw gives ~2,000 effects; their 2.5th/97.5th percentiles are the 95% interval, and the p-value is how often the simulated pooled counterfactual lands on the wrong side of the actual. This is BSTS re-rolling its own forecast uncertainty ~2,000 times, not resampling advertisers the way the DiD bootstrap does.

### DiD, in three rungs

**Rung 1 — the 2×2 atom.** 

For one cohort vs a control group:

$$\text{DiD Lift} = \frac{\text{treated}_{\text{post}} / \text{treated}_{\text{pre}}}{\text{control}_{\text{post}} / \text{control}_{\text{pre}}} - 1$$

The control's growth divides out market-wide drift, so what's left is the treatment's own effect. Each rate is `Σnumerator / Σdenominator` (e.g. IVR = visits / impressions) pooled over the pre-window (the `did_pre_days=14` days before the flip) and the post-window (the day after the flip through today; the flip day itself falls in neither).

**Rung 2 — pooling + bootstrap.** 

For a single cohort, the point estimate pools every treated advertiser into one treated rate and every control advertiser into one control rate, then takes the ratio of their growth. Eg. For IVR, we calculate the point estimate as:

$$\text{DiD Lift} = \frac{\dfrac{\Sigma\,\text{treated visits}_{\text{post}} / \Sigma\,\text{treated impr}_{\text{post}}}{\Sigma\,\text{treated visits}_{\text{pre}} / \Sigma\,\text{treated impr}_{\text{pre}}}}{\dfrac{\Sigma\,\text{control visits}_{\text{post}} / \Sigma\,\text{control impr}_{\text{post}}}{\Sigma\,\text{control visits}_{\text{pre}} / \Sigma\,\text{control impr}_{\text{pre}}}} - 1$$

The **interval** is where the advertisers get resampled. Across 1,000 draws, resample *which advertisers are in the pool* (with replacement, 1,000 samples of treated and 1,000 samples of control drawn separately), pull each drawn advertiser in as a whole block of counts, then **re-sum those counts and recompute the pooled ratio-of-ratios from scratch** each draw. We keep the 2.5th/97.5th percentiles of the 1,000 recomputed lifts to create the 95% CI, and the two-sided p is how often a draw lands on the wrong side of zero (doubled). The point estimate never moves; the bootstrap only puts a spread around it.

**Rung 3 — staggered cohorts + clean-holdout control.** 

Waves flip on different dates, so you cannot throw every advertiser into one big 2×2: a single calendar cutoff would land inside a late cohort's pre-period and mislabel its not-yet-treated days as "post," and each cohort has to be judged against how the market drifted *over its own window*. So each cohort keeps its own flip date, gets its own before/after split and its own control drift, and the cohorts are combined by **pooling counts, not rates**.

**The pooled effect, step by step.** For each cohort, the treated and control before/after windows give these numbers (shown with IVR, whose rate is visits ÷ impressions):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{treated\_pre\_rate}    &= \text{treated visits before} \div \text{treated impressions before} \\
\text{treated\_post\_volume} &= \text{treated impressions after} \quad (\text{post-flip denominator}) \\
\text{actual\_post}          &= \text{treated visits after} \quad (\text{numerator: what actually happened}) \\
\text{control\_pre\_rate}    &= \text{control visits before} \div \text{control impressions before} \\
\text{control\_post\_rate}   &= \text{control visits after} \div \text{control impressions after} \\
\text{market\_drift}         &= \text{control\_post\_rate} \div \text{control\_pre\_rate}
\end{aligned}
$$

Turn each cohort into a **counterfactual count**, the visits you would expect with no treatment:

$$\text{counterfactual\_post} = \text{treated\_pre\_rate} \times \text{market\_drift} \times \text{treated\_post\_volume}$$

That is two multiplications: `treated_pre_rate × market_drift` is the rate the cohort would have run at with no treatment (its old efficiency, moved by the market), and `× treated_post_volume` turns that rate into an expected number of visits. Then pool across cohorts and take one ratio:

$$\text{pooled\_lift} = \frac{\sum \text{actual\_post}}{\sum \text{counterfactual\_post}} \; - \; 1 \qquad (\text{sums taken across all cohorts})$$

Worked, two cohorts:

```
Cohort 1:  treated_pre_rate 100/1000 = 0.100
           market_drift              = 1.10
           treated_post_volume       = 600

           actual_post               = 80
           
           counterfactual_post = 0.100 × 1.10 × 600 = 66

Cohort 2:  treated_pre_rate  50/500  = 0.100
           market_drift              = 1.20
           treated_post_volume       = 750

           actual_post               = 90

           counterfactual_post = 0.100 × 1.20 × 750 = 90

Pooled:    Σ actual_post = 80 + 90 = 170,  Σ counterfactual_post = 156   →   170 / 156 − 1 = +9.0%
```

**Control and interval.** The 95% interval comes from resampling advertisers 1,000 times, treated and control drawn independently each round. The **treated** sample is drawn from all treated advertisers pooled across every cohort, so a pick can be any advertiser from any cohort and just counts toward its own cohort. The **control** sample is drawn from the whole holdout, and each drawn control advertiser counts its before/after separately for every cohort, using that cohort's window.

Worked, with treated **T1, T2** in Cohort A (flip Jan 15), **T3, T4** in Cohort B (flip Jan 25), and holdout **C1, C2, C3**:

- **Treated draw:** 4 picks from `{T1, T2, T3, T4}` with replacement, e.g. `{T1, T1, T3, T4}`, so this round Cohort A = T1 twice and Cohort B = T3, T4. Which cohort each pick lands in just follows the advertiser.
- **Control draw:** 3 picks from `{C1, C2, C3}` with replacement, e.g. `{C1, C1, C2}`, and this one sample feeds both cohorts. C1 was drawn twice, so it counts twice in Cohort A (before-window Jan 1–14, after Jan 15 on) and twice in Cohort B (before-window Jan 11–24, after Jan 25 on). Same advertiser, a different window in each cohort.

That draw then runs through the **same count-pool as the point estimate above**: within each cohort, sum the drawn advertisers' counts (a pick drawn twice is added twice) to get `treated_pre_rate`, the drawn control's `market_drift` over that cohort's window, and `treated_post_volume`; form `counterfactual_post = treated_pre_rate × market_drift × treated_post_volume`; then pool `Σ actual_post / Σ counterfactual_post − 1` across cohorts. For this draw, Cohort A's inputs come from `{T1, T1}` treated and `{C1, C1, C2}` control, Cohort B's from `{T3, T4}` and the same `{C1, C1, C2}`. One lift per draw; the middle 95% of the 1,000 lifts is the interval.

A single-cohort rollout has just one treated bucket plus the holdout, so its "All Treated" equals that cohort's own bar.

**The parallel-trends line.** It already used the static holdout, so under the clean-holdout default it agrees with the point/CI control — one fixed-membership yardstick.

**Small cohorts.** The treated resample is pooled across cohorts rather than drawn within each, so how much a given cohort is represented in a draw is itself random, and a very small cohort can drop out of some draws entirely. This only widens the pooled interval, never tightens it, so the read errs conservative, most visibly when a small-count cohort carries large volume. Resampling within each cohort would remove that wobble, but it would then understate how little a 1-3 advertiser cohort actually tells you, so we keep the pooled draw as the default. When a tiny cohort might be driving the headline, trust its own forest bar and the per-advertiser spread over the pooled interval.

### What metrics are measured?

IVR, CPV, CVR, CPA, and ROAS. **All five are fit independently** under both methods

### Advertiser eligibility (which advertisers get measured)

Advertisers do messy things — pause, restart, change budgets — so before either method runs, a **single per-advertiser eligibility gate** decides who is trustworthy enough to measure. It is applied **identically to BSTS and DiD** (cell `eligibility` builds `ELIGIBLE_AIDS`; `fit-all` and `did-driver` both filter to it), so the two methods measure the same roster and the 3-Point view stays apples-to-apples. A treated advertiser is **eligible** when all hold:

- **Minimum Impression Volume (Pre and Post)** - `min_window_impressions` (default 1000) — a trivial-volume floor **symmetric across treated + control**. This is control's *only* gate.
- **Minimum Active Days Before Flip** - `min_pre_days` (default 14) counted within the last `pre_active_window_days` days (default 25) — enough *recent* active (impression-bearing) days to establish "normal." Default is at least 14 days active over the 25 days before the flip.
- **Minimum Active Days After Flip** - `min_post_active_days` (default 1, **always**) — at least one active post-day; do not measure a zero-delivery post-period.
- **Minimum Active Days After Maturity Window** - `min_mature_post_active_days` (defaults 4) — Once the cohort has passed the maturity window (`maturity_days`). The advertiser must be active at least 4 days

### The config knobs — what each one means

The BQ table `dw-main-silver.experiments.causal_experiment` contains 1 row per experiment and holds all of the relevant configuration settings to make small tweaks experiment-to-experiment. So a team can tune any of them per rollout with **no code change to the dashboard itself**. Read this as the lever reference for anyone onboarding a new experiment:

| Knob (`config column` / *Dataset name*) | Default | Category | What it controls, in plain terms |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ci_pre_days` / *Ci Pre Days* | 60 | Measurement window | How far back the daily panel pulls pre-flip history for BSTS to learn the advertiser's normal pattern (baseline level + weekly rhythm). Applied SQL-side from the **earliest** flip across treated, so a later-flipping cohort can carry a bit more than 60 days; the notebook then fits on all the pre-flip days it receives (no per-advertiser 60-day cutoff). Longer = more baseline. |
| `did_pre_days` / *Did Pre Days* | 14 | Measurement window | How many days before the flip DiD averages to get the "before" rate for treated + control. Deliberately shorter than BSTS — DiD only needs a stable *recent* baseline, not a full seasonal fit. |
| `bsts_harmonics` / *Bsts Harmonics* | 2 | Model shape | How much weekly (day-of-week) seasonality the BSTS model fits. `2` captures the dominant weekday/weekend swing; higher gets wigglier and risks overfitting short pre-periods. |
| `maturity_days` / *Maturity Days* | 14 | Maturity | How long after the flip before a result is "settled." Set to the conversion attribution window (~2 weeks). Drives both the "Mature only" cohort view **and** the eligibility dark-filter trigger. |
| `min_pre_days` / *Min Pre Days* | 14 | Eligibility | Fewest **active (impression-bearing)** days, counted within the `pre_active_window_days` look-back, an advertiser needs to be measured. No baseline → no counterfactual. Both methods. |
| `pre_active_window_days` / *Pre Active Window Days* | 25 | Eligibility | The look-back window (days before flip) that the `min_pre_days` active days are counted within. Decoupled from `ci_pre_days` (2026-07-09) so an advertiser active only *early* in the 60-day BSTS window, then dark near the flip, fails the gate. Keep `min_pre_days` ≤ this ≤ `ci_pre_days`. |
| `min_post_active_days` / *Min Post Active Days* | 1 | Eligibility | Fewest active post-flip days, always. `1` = don't measure an advertiser that flipped but never delivered. |
| `min_mature_post_active_days` / *Min Mature Post Active Days* | 4 | Eligibility | Once an advertiser has been live ≥ `maturity_days`, it must have delivered on at least this many days — else it's "mature but dark" and dropped. |
| `min_window_impressions` / *Min Window Impressions* | 1000 | Eligibility | Fewest total impressions over the whole window; drops trivial-volume / scheduled-but-dark advertisers. Applied to treated **and** control (enforced in SQL 02/05). |
| `measurement_end_date` / *Measurement End Date* | NULL | Freeze | `NULL` = read through today (live). A date **freezes** the whole experiment (treatment + control) at that day so a closed experiment's numbers stop drifting and stay reproducible (C10). |

Truly-global engine constants (simulation counts, `ALPHA`, VIF threshold) stay in the notebook, not config. The BSTS simulation seed is derived per-experiment from the experiment key, so runs are reproducible yet distinct experiments draw distinct paths.

## Part 3 — the charts, one by one

Every visual in the dashboard, taken left tab to right and top to bottom: a shot of the chart and a short note on **how its number is made**. Read 3.0 first (the conventions every chart shares), then jump to the view you care about. Three color-coded views: **BSTS** (teal), **Difference-in-Differences** (violet), and **3-Point Analysis** (amber, which triangulates the two methods against the naive baseline).

### 3.0 Conventions every chart shares

**Significance = the 95% interval excludes zero.** A ⭐ marks that; ⚪️ is borderline (0.05 ≤ p < 0.10); blank is not significant. The p-value shown beside it is the two-sided tail probability from the **same draws that produced the interval** (the BSTS posterior simulation, or the DiD bootstrap). They usually point the same way, but a BSTS p-value and its interval come from slightly different variance constructions and can disagree at the margin, so the ⭐ is gated on the interval: it requires **both** that the interval exclude zero **and** p < 0.05. (That gate is also why ⚪️ is rare: it needs a marginal p whose interval still clears zero.) The star is only a yes/no shortcut, while the interval also shows the effect's size and its uncertainty, so **read the interval.**

**When you get a tested p-value, and when you don't.** This resampling is costly and would need to be redone with every combination of cohorts, so to save time - we do not run statistical analysis on every combination of cohorts. Instead we run them for:
1. Each Individual Cohort
2. All "Mature" Cohorts (a cohort with at least 14 days of data post-flip)
3. All Cohorts (Including the Non-Matured cohorts)

 Pick any *other* hand-mixed subset and the dashboard still shows the correctly pooled results but shows `p = —`, because you cannot validly average p-values across separately-fit models.
 
### BSTS view (teal)

BSTS (Bayesian structural time series) builds the counterfactual by **forecasting** what each treated series would have done without the flip, from its own pre-flip baseline level and weekly seasonality (plus an optional market covariate); the effect is actual minus forecast.

#### Headline lift + verdict (CI-1)

![BSTS headline cards](data:image/png;base64,)

One card per headline metric, each with the lift, its 95% interval, the p-value, the advertiser count, and the naive before/after for contrast. 

**How it's made:** the Part 2 recipe. One BSTS fit on the pre-flip days, forecast the counterfactual, effect = avg actual rate ÷ avg counterfactual − 1; the interval is the ~2,000 simulated counterfactuals (one cohort) or their flip-clock pool (multiple cohorts). A card colors green or red only when its interval clears zero. The **"vs naive"** line reports the plain before/after change on the same pre/post windows (no counterfactual); placed beside the causal effect, the gap between the two is the correction the method applied.

#### Actual vs counterfactual (CI-2)

![Actual vs counterfactual, one chart per cohort](data:image/png;base64,)

One chart per cohort: the actual daily rate (solid) against the forecast counterfactual (dashed), a 95% band, and a flip marker. 

**How it's made:** the dashed line is the fitted pre-flip recipe (baseline level + weekly pattern + optional covariate) run forward on each post day; the band re-rolls the model's residual noise ~2,000 times and takes the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile per day, so it widens the further past the flip you look. 

**Read it:** judge the fit by how tightly the dashed tracks the solid *before* the flip; after it, the solid pulling clear of the band is the effect.

#### Lift by cohort (CI-3)

![BSTS lift-by-cohort forest plot](data:image/png;base64,)

A forest plot, one box per cohort (box = 95% interval, marker = point estimate). 

**How it's made:** the same per-cohort numbers as CI-1, drawn as boxes so you can compare waves side by side (no new computation). Green clears zero the good way, red the bad way, gray straddles it. 

**Read it:** younger cohorts have fewer post days, so wider boxes (less certainty, not a weaker effect), and the pooled "All Treated" box should sit within the spread of the per-cohort boxes.

#### Daily & cumulative effect (CI-4)

![Daily and cumulative effect since flip, with milestones](data:image/png;base64,)

Daily effect bars, a cumulative line, Day 7 / 21 / 42 milestone tiles, and a "% of post-flip days moved the right way" stat. 

**How it's made:** cohorts are aligned on their own flip clocks; the daily effect at day *k* is Σ actual counts ÷ Σ counterfactual counts − 1 across the cohorts live that day (a count = rate × that day's volume). The cumulative point through day K averages those per-day pooled rates with **equal weight across days** (a running mean of the daily actual rates ÷ a running mean of the daily counterfactual rates − 1); this is the same recipe as the headline, so the line's last point equals the CI-1 headline and each day counts the same regardless of its volume. The full step-by-step is below. 

**Read it:** the mix thins to the right as younger cohorts run out, and a jump right after a drop-off is a change in *who* is measured, not the effect. And because the cumulative line is a running *average* (not a running total), it moves toward each new day's effect: a positive day that lands below the average-so-far still pulls the line down, and the line rises only when a day beats the effect to date.

**How the cumulative line is built, step by step.** The daily bars and the cumulative line come from the same per-cohort daily series (`BSTS Daily Cohort`: one row per cohort × metric × day-since-flip, each carrying that day's actual rate, counterfactual rate, and volume). It is a **two-stage pool: volume-weighted *within* a day, equal-weighted *across* days.** This is the Part 2 multi-cohort BSTS pooling recipe, walked one day at a time.

*Stage 1, within a day (volume-weighted across cohorts).* Line the cohorts up on the flip clock (each on its own day-since-flip). For each day *k*, sum across the cohorts live that day:

```
actNum[k]  = Σ (actual rate × volume)          pooled actual count that day
cfNum[k]   = Σ (counterfactual rate × volume)  pooled counterfactual count
volume[k]  = Σ volume
```

The per-day pooled rates are the ratios: `pooledActual[k] = actNum[k] / volume[k]` and `pooledCf[k] = cfNum[k] / volume[k]`. A bigger cohort pulls that day's pooled rate toward itself. **The daily bar is those two divided:** `pooledActual[k] / pooledCf[k] − 1`.

*Stage 2, across days (equal-weighted).* Accumulate the per-day pooled rates with a running sum, then take the ratio:

$$\text{cumulative through day } K \;=\; \frac{\sum_{k \le K} \text{pooledActual}[k]}{\sum_{k \le K} \text{pooledCf}[k]} \;-\; 1$$

The day-count cancels in that ratio, so it equals (mean pooled actual rate) ÷ (mean pooled counterfactual rate) − 1 over days 0..K: **every day counts once, regardless of its volume.** Two weightings on purpose: volume within a day (a big cohort matters more), equal across days (one high-volume day cannot dominate the trajectory).

Worked, two cohorts (IVR: rate = visits ÷ impressions, volume = impressions). First, pool the live cohorts within each day:

| Day | Live cohorts (rate, cf, impressions) | pooledActual | pooledCf |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---:|
| 1 | A (0.10, 0.08, 3000) and B (0.20, 0.15, 1000) | 0.125 | 0.0975 |
| 2 | same as Day 1 | 0.125 | 0.0975 |
| 3 | A only (0.11, 0.08) | 0.110 | 0.080 |

Day 1 shows the volume weighting: `pooledActual = (0.10×3000 + 0.20×1000) / 4000 = 0.125` and `pooledCf = (0.08×3000 + 0.15×1000) / 4000 = 0.0975`.

Then accumulate the per-day pooled rates with equal weight across days:

| Through | Σ pooledActual | Σ pooledCf | cumulative (ratio − 1) |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---|
| Day 1 | 0.125 | 0.0975 | 0.125 / 0.0975 − 1 = **+28.2%** |
| Day 2 | 0.250 | 0.1950 | +28.2% (Day 2 repeats Day 1, so no move) |
| Day 3 | 0.360 | 0.2750 | 0.360 / 0.2750 − 1 = **+30.9%** |

That +30.9% endpoint is the same pooled effect the Part 2 example lands on, and it is what the CI-1 headline reports (the last point equals the headline by construction). The **Day 7 / 21 / 42 milestone tiles** are this same ratio stopped at day *N*, i.e. "the headline-style effect as of day *N*."

*Why a positive day can still pull the line down.* Because the cumulative is a running average, each new day moves it toward that day's own effect. In the example, Day 3's own effect is `0.11 / 0.08 − 1 = +37.5%`, above the running +28.2%, so it pulls the line up. A day that lands *below* the running average, even a positive one, pulls it down; the line rises only when a day beats the effect-to-date.

#### Per-advertiser spread (CI-5)

![BSTS per-advertiser effect histogram](data:image/png;base64,)

A histogram of the per-advertiser effects plus four counts (significantly / directionally, each worse / better); answers "broad-based, or carried by a few?" 

**How it's made:** every advertiser gets its own BSTS fit (the CI-1 engine, one advertiser at a time, ~1,000 sims each), then is bucketed by its own significance and direction. The histogram is the spread of those effects (zero-centered, axis clipped at the 5th/95th percentile, significant advertisers darker), and the denominator is the true advertiser count, not just those that fit. 

**Read it:** a headline resting on a few dark bars far from zero is weaker than one spread across many.

**Drilldowns (CI-5b / CI-6 / CI-7).**

![BSTS drilldowns: per-advertiser table, diagnostics, and excluded advertisers](data:image/png;base64,)

Three collapsible sections at the foot of the view, none with new computation: **CI-5b** tabulates the per-advertiser fits behind CI-5 (searchable, sortable); **CI-6** summarizes fit quality across those fits (convergence is the pass/fail signal, MAPE and interval width are context); **CI-7** lists the treated advertisers the eligibility gate hard-excluded, with the reason (immature-but-kept advertisers are flagged elsewhere, not here).

### Difference-in-Differences view (violet)

DiD builds the counterfactual from a **control group** instead of a forecast: the treated group's before→after change divided by the control's before→after change, so shared market drift cancels and the treatment's own effect is left.

#### Headline lift + verdict (DiD-1)

![DiD headline cards](data:image/png;base64,)

A summary strip (treated / control counts, post length) and one card per metric (lift, 95% interval, p, treated-vs-control counts). 

**How it's made:** DiD lift = (treated post ÷ treated pre) ÷ (control post ÷ control pre) − 1, with the interval and p from the advertiser-clustered bootstrap (Part 2, Rungs 2 to 3). Same green/red-only-when-significant coloring and same p rule as BSTS: a single cohort, All, or All Mature carry a tested p; other subsets show `p = —`.

#### Parallel trends (DiD-2)

![Parallel trends, treated vs control](data:image/png;base64,)

Treated (solid) and control (dashed) pooled daily rates over days since flip, with the flip marked. 

**How it's made:** just the two pooled daily rate series; this is the *assumption check* DiD rests on, not a new estimate. 

**Read it:** before the flip the two lines should move together (parallel), which is what makes the control a fair counterfactual; after it, the gap that opens is the effect. Read by eye today, no pre-trend p-value is computed yet (top of the deferred list in [DRIFT.md](DRIFT.md)).

#### Lift by cohort (DiD-3)

![DiD lift-by-cohort forest plot](data:image/png;base64,)

The violet twin of CI-3, one box per cohort (box = 95% bootstrap interval, marker = point). 

**How it's made:** each cohort's DiD lift with its bootstrap interval (the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile of the resamples). 

**Read it:** same as CI-3, a box clearing zero is significant and younger waves are wider.

#### Per-advertiser spread (DiD-4)

![DiD per-advertiser effect histogram](data:image/png;base64,)

Two directional counts (better / worse vs control), a histogram, and a drilldown table. 

**How it's made:** each advertiser's own before→after change, net of the control's drift. There is **no per-advertiser significance** here, because DiD's inference is the cohort-level clustered bootstrap (it needs the whole cohort), so this view is descriptive. 

**Read it:** use it to see whether a cohort's DiD is broad-based or carried by a few, then go to DiD-3 for the significance verdict.

**Drilldown table.**

![DiD per-advertiser drilldown table](data:image/png;base64,)

The searchable, sortable table of every advertiser's own DiD lift (the numbers behind the histogram above).

### 3-Point Analysis view (amber)

Three methods, three assumption sets: the **naive** before/after, **BSTS** (forecast counterfactual), and **DiD** (control-group counterfactual). When they point the same way, the read is robust to method choice. This view compares **direction only**; it never pools the p-values into a combined test.

#### Do the methods agree? (Syn-1)

![Three-method consensus cards](data:image/png;base64,)

One card per metric with all three reads (naive / BSTS / DiD), each signed and starred where significant, plus a badge: "3/3 agree," "2/3 lean," "methods split," or "no estimate." 

**How it's made:** each method's own estimate from its section above; agreement is simply whether they share the same sign. 

**Read it:** a unanimous card is the strongest read here; "split" is the one worth digging into.

#### Effect size with intervals (Syn-2)

![Overlaid BSTS and DiD effect-size forest](data:image/png;base64,)

Per metric, BSTS (teal) and DiD (violet) as point + 95% interval, with the naive read as a marker. 

**How it's made:** the two methods' intervals from their own sections drawn on one axis; naive has no interval because it is a raw before/after, not a modeled estimate. 

**Read it:** both intervals on the same side of zero means the methods converge; a wide interval that still clears zero is a small-sample cohort, not a weaker effect.

#### Naive vs BSTS vs DiD (Syn-3)

![Three-method comparison table](data:image/png;base64,)

A table of all three reads per cohort and metric, each cell colored by direction and shown solid + bold where significant (faded where not); the three methods share identical styling, with no stars and no column emphasized over another. 

**How it's made:** the three estimates side by side (no new computation); one toggle expands a pooled selection into its member cohorts, another adds direction glyphs. 

**Read it:** where all three agree in sign and rough magnitude, the read is robust to method choice.

### 3.4 Around the charts (header, sidebar, data quality)

- **Header** names the experiment and shows **"N measured of N seeded advertisers"** (measured = passed the eligibility gate), plus the flip-date range and the scope label.
- **Sidebar** holds the cohort selector (with the young-cohort caution marker) and a short plain-language BSTS-vs-DiD explainer.
- **Data quality** panel restates how many advertisers were measured vs filtered in the current selection, broken down by exclusion reason — the transparency counterpart to CI-7.
- **Status bar** names the source config table, the two methods, and the reminder that the 3-Point view is directional agreement, not a combined significance test.
